passage:
Subject: my timetable is ruined
Siddharth bhaiya,
You know my board-exam timetable, the one with green for physics, blue for maths and every half hour planned till March. On Saturday Mausi's flight was delayed, and we all went to fetch her from the airport at midnight. I lost the whole Sunday to sleep. I felt so guilty that I cancelled my cricket for the next two weeks to "pay it back" and stayed up till two redoing the colour codes. Today I could barely read one page. Amma says I'm punishing myself. Maybe. You topped your boards. Did you ever lose a day? How did you not panic?
Saurabh

qa.q: What colour did Saurabh use for physics?
Why did Saurabh cancel cricket for two weeks?
qa.a: Saurabh felt guilty about the lost Sunday and wanted to "pay it back", treating rest as something to be punished.

qa.q: What went wrong after the lost Sunday, and what could Saurabh try instead?
qa.a: Staying up till two to redo the codes left Saurabh barely able to read; simply moving the lost work into the coming week would cost less.

qa.q: How might Amma feel watching Saurabh this week?
qa.a: Amma seems worried to see hard work turning into self-punishment, which is why she says so out loud.

grounding: A teenager with a colour-coded exam timetable feels guilty over one unplanned day and turns the plan into self-punishment.

passage:
Afreen asked, "Dhruv, why did you look like a ghost all last week?"
Honestly, Afreen, the planner is the best thing about me. Six colours, every chapter mapped, and I've never missed a deadline. But last Tuesday Nani turned eighty and the house filled with cousins. No studying. I smiled through the cake and felt sick the whole time, like I was stealing hours. That night I set an alarm for four to make up for it, and the next night too. By Thursday I was reading the same paragraph again and again and snapping at my little brother. You know what finally hit me? The planner had no row for Nani. I'd made a plan that could only break, never bend. So now I'm trying something scary: Sundays left blank.

qa.q: How many colours does Dhruv's planner use?
What was Dhruv feeling during Nani's birthday cake?
qa.a: Dhruv felt guilty and sick, as if the family hours were being stolen from study.

qa.q: What turning point does Dhruv reach about the planner?
qa.a: Dhruv notices it had no row for Nani and decides to leave Sundays blank, so the plan can bend instead of break.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's little brother have experienced that week?
qa.a: Being snapped at by a tired older sibling probably hurt, with no way of knowing it came from the four o'clock alarms.

grounding: A teenager proud of a detailed study planner feels guilty after an unplanned family day and answers it with punishing early alarms before seeing the plan must bend.
